notes: The line reads like a translation of Camus ('j'etais absent au moment ou je prenais le plus de place') and is thematically consistent with the self-accusing narrator of La Chute (The Fall, 1956) or the Carnets. I cannot place it in a specific work or confirm the translation, and I will not name a book I am not sure of. Attribution to Camus is plausible and consistently made, but unverified.

earliest_print_source: Farewell Address at Springfield, Illinois, February 11, 1861; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. IV
notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the Springfield farewell remarks delivered on departing for Washington. The documented wording is 'Without the assistance of that Divine Being, who ever attended him, I cannot succeed. With that assistance I cannot fail.' The corpus text is a lightly trimmed version of that sentence; the substance and the source event are secure.

A very widely repeated Lincoln line, but it rests on later recollection rather than a contemporaneous document. It circulates via post-assassination memoirs and religious biographies of Lincoln, and reference works generally file it under attributed rather than sourced. Lincoln is a known misattribution magnet, so I am holding this below the promotion bar; the sentiment fits his recorded remarks about religion, but no primary source is in my knowledge.

'Adept Godrakpa' is the distinctive rendering used for Gotsangpa Gonpo Dorje (1189-1258), the Tibetan Kagyu yogi, in Cyrus Stearns' translation of his songs of realization published by Wisdom Publications around 2000. The imagery (body like spring mist, mind like empty sky, thoughts like breezes) and the three-point contemplative structure match that body of doggerel-song instruction closely, so the attribution is probably right. I am not certain enough of the exact page or the exact translated wording to record a print citation, so the source field stays null.

Alan Cohen is a prolific inspirational author (The Dragon Doesn't Live Here Anymore, Wisdom of the Heart) whose aphorisms circulate through books, newsletters, and daily-quote services with consistent attribution but almost never with a book-and-page citation. Attribution is plausible and uncontested; no primary source in my knowledge.

Same situation as the other Alan Cohen aphorisms in this batch: consistently attributed to him across quote collections, no traceable first appearance in my knowledge. Nothing suggests a different author; the uncertainty is about sourcing, not about who wrote it.

Widely circulated as Alan Cohen, typically without citation. The left-brain/right-brain framing places it in the late-twentieth-century self-help idiom he writes in, which is consistent with the attribution, but I cannot locate a specific book or column.

Attributed to Alan Cohen wherever I have seen it, with no source given. Short enough and aphoristic enough that provenance drift is easy; I have no evidence of an earlier or different author, but no evidence for the attribution beyond repetition either.

Attributed to Alan Cohen without citation. Worth flagging that the idea, and nearly the phrasing, is central to Anthony de Mello's Awareness ('spirituality means waking up... most people are asleep and don't know it'), so this may be a restatement of de Mello that acquired Cohen's name, or a genuine Cohen line in the same lineage. I cannot tell which, so I am not proposing a reattribution.

Consistently attributed to Alan Cohen and one of his more frequently reproduced lines, which slightly strengthens the attribution, but I can point to no book, essay, or dated appearance. Sourcing unverified.
Attributed to Alan Cohen in quote collections with no citation. Voice and vocabulary are consistent with his other work; nothing more than that supports it.

This is a Buddhist scriptural formula, not an Alan Watts original. The line 'Things are not what they seem, nor are they otherwise' is a well-known rendering from the Lankavatara Sutra, and Watts quoted this kind of formulation in his writing on Zen and Mahayana. Attributing it to Watts credits the popularizer rather than the source. My confidence is in the Lankavatara provenance of the formula; I cannot confirm which translation this exact English wording comes from, and it is possible Watts's own paraphrase is what circulates.
suggested_reattribution: Lankavatara Sutra (as quoted/paraphrased by Alan Watts)

earliest_print_source: Letter to Isham Reavis, November 5, 1855; Collected Works of Abraham Lincoln, Vol. II
notes: Genuine Lincoln, from the letter of advice to Isham Reavis, a young man who had asked about studying law. The documented wording is 'Always bear in mind that your own resolution to succeed, is more important than any other one thing'; the corpus text drops 'other'. I am confident about the letter and the recipient; consider restoring the original wording.

earliest_print_source: 'Principles of Research', address at Max Planck's 60th birthday celebration, Physical Society, Berlin, 1918; reprinted in Ideas and Opinions (1954)
notes: Authentic Einstein from the 1918 Planck birthday address, one of his best-documented statements about how physical theory is actually arrived at. Original reads 'no logical way to the discovery of these elemental laws'; the corpus text drops 'these'. Source and occasion are secure.

I cannot place this in Alan Watts's books or recorded talks. The idea (a mind in its natural state, unfixed and therefore able to respond in any direction) is standard mushin/wu-hsin material that Watts wrote about in The Way of Zen, and the phrasing also resembles English renderings of Takuan Soho's The Unfettered Mind, which Watts drew on. That makes the attribution plausible but unsupported. Possibly a paraphrase of Watts rather than his words.

No source in Einstein's writings, letters, or interviews that I know of; reference compilations of Einstein quotations treat it as attributed rather than sourced. The sentiment closely tracks a documented Niels Bohr remark to Wolfgang Pauli ('we are all agreed that your theory is crazy; the question is whether it is crazy enough to have a chance of being correct'), and this may be a compressed folk version of that exchange re-badged with Einstein's name. I cannot establish the true origin, so no reattribution.

This reads as authentic Einstein prose and I recall it from collections of his writings on the religious feeling of the scientist, associated with his early-1930s credo material ('Mein Glaubensbekenntnis' / The World As I See It). The distinctive cadence and the 'neither evolution nor eternity, only being' close are hard to fake and are consistent with his German essays in translation. I am confident enough in authorship to call it attributed, but I cannot pin the exact essay or year, so I am leaving the citation null and staying under the promotion bar.

I have no record of this in Einstein's writings, and it sits awkwardly against his documented positions, which consistently favour inquiry over belief and reject the 'better to believe' framing as such. It circulates mainly through quotation websites. Einstein is the single largest misattribution magnet in the corpus; absent any source, this should not be promoted.

I believe this is authentic Einstein, from his mid-1930s statements collected in The World As I See It / Mein Weltbild, and it is quoted with consistent wording in serious Einstein compilations rather than only on quote sites. The phrase 'love and devotion towards men and towards objective things' is a characteristic translation of his German. I cannot confirm the specific essay or letter, so the citation stays null and I am holding below 0.80.

Authentic Einstein as far as I know it. The fuller passage continues 'It cannot lead, it can only serve; and it is not fastidious in its choice of a leader', and it appears in the standard English collections of his essays (Ideas and Opinions / Out of My Later Years). The extended, coherent context is good evidence of genuineness. I am not certain enough which original essay or year it comes from to record an earliest print source, so it sits just under the promotion bar pending a human check against Ideas and Opinions.

Almost certainly a paraphrase rather than Einstein's words. What is documented is his 1946 campaign for atomic-age rethinking: 'The unleashed power of the atom has changed everything save our modes of thinking, and thus we drift toward unparalleled catastrophe', and 'a new type of thinking is essential if mankind is to survive'. This line compresses that into modern self-help phrasing. No source for this exact wording. Closely related to q_0243 below, which is the better-known version of the same drift.

One of the most-repeated Einstein misattributions and a documented case of quote drift. It has no source in Einstein's writings; the wording appears in late-twentieth-century management, therapy, and self-help literature and was retro-attributed to him, evolving out of his genuine 1946 remarks about needing a new mode of thinking in the atomic age. Quote-investigation work and the standard Einstein quotation reference both place it in the unsourced/misattributed category. No identifiable individual author, so apocryphal rather than a reattribution.

I am fairly confident this is authentic. The German original is known ('Wer sich als Richter auf dem Gebiete der Wahrheit und Erkenntnis aufzuwerfen unternimmt, wird vom Gelaechter der Goetter zerschmettert'), which is strong evidence against a modern English-language invention, and it is generally dated to an Einstein aphorism of the early 1950s. I cannot confirm the publication it first appeared in, so no citation and no promotion; a human check against the standard Einstein quotation reference should settle it.

Consistently attributed to Einstein and compatible with his documented views on social obligation ('a hundred times every day I remind myself that my inner and outer life are based on the labors of other men'), but I cannot place this specific sentence in any of his writings or interviews. The plain, proverbial phrasing is the kind that attracts famous names. Attribution plausible, sourcing absent.

Correctly pre-flagged. There is no Einstein source for this; it does not appear in his published writings, letters, or interviews, and the standard Einstein quotation reference lists it among sayings attributed to him without support. Attributions to Einstein surface long after his death and appear to be a rebadging of an older inspirational commonplace. No identifiable original author, so apocryphal.
